\chapter{Courtesy and Responses}
\label{ch:greetings}
\hlchaptermodality{2}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can thank someone, take my leave, answer yes or no, say that something is good, write \gu{હા} from a heard cue, and retrieve the seven pieces needed to read \gu{આભાર}.}

Complete GU-C01-practice, choose an appropriate courtesy or response, retrieve \gu{હા} from sound, and write the seven pieces needed to read \gu{આભાર} with no visible model.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ra]{\gu{ર} — one new shape, ra}

\label{lesson:GU-W02-ra}



\begin{quote}
Say the inherent-vowel rule once: a bare Gujarati consonant carries short \emph{a}. Keep that rule; add only one shape.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — meet the shape}
Keep \textbf{\gu{ર}} visible. It is \textbf{ra}: \emph{r} plus the inherent \emph{a}. Begin at the upper left, circle clockwise around the rounded upper body, continue through the small middle loop, and descend into the lower-right tail without lifting.

\subsection*{Writing — notice and trace}
Finger-trace \textbf{\gu{ર}} once. Then trace it once in the air. Say \emph{ra} only after the motion stops.

\subsection*{Writing — copy with the model}
Keep \textbf{\gu{ર}} visible and copy it once. Compare only three landmarks: rounded top, small middle loop, descending tail. If one differs, repair that part.

\subsection*{Writing — recall after hiding}
Cover the model. Write \emph{ra} once from memory, then uncover \textbf{\gu{ર}} and check the three landmarks. Stop after one honest repair.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What vowel comes free with \textbf{\gu{ર}}? (\textbf{Short a.}) Name the three landmarks without writing again. (\textbf{Rounded top, small loop, descending tail.})

Sources: \href{https://www.t30apps.com/gujarati-alphabet-writing/}{Gujarati Alphabet Writing Practice} and the \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0A80.pdf}{Unicode Gujarati chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[da]{\gu{દ} — one continuous shape, da}

\label{lesson:GU-W02-da}



\begin{quote}
Without looking back, write \textbf{\gu{ર}} once. Check it, then set it aside.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — meet the shape}
Keep \textbf{\gu{દ}} visible. It is \textbf{da}. Begin at the upper right, circle the rounded upper body into the narrow middle turn, then continue without lifting around the broad lower body and rise into the compact right terminal.

\subsection*{Writing — notice and trace}
Finger-trace \textbf{\gu{દ}} once, then air-trace it once. One continuous run; no lift.

\subsection*{Writing — copy with the model}
Copy visible \textbf{\gu{દ}} once. Check upper round, narrow turn, broad lower round. Repair only the landmark that differs.

\subsection*{Writing — recall after hiding}
Hide the model and write \emph{da} once. Uncover \textbf{\gu{દ}}, compare, and stop after one repair.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many pen lifts? (\textbf{None.}) What vowel is already present? (\textbf{a.})

Sources: \href{https://www.t30apps.com/gujarati-alphabet-writing/}{Gujarati Alphabet Writing Practice} and the \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0A80.pdf}{Unicode Gujarati chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[va]{\gu{વ} — rounded body, separate spine, va}

\label{lesson:GU-W02-va}



\begin{quote}
Write \textbf{\gu{દ}} once from memory. Then look at the new model only.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — meet the shape}
Keep \textbf{\gu{વ}} visible. It is \textbf{va}. Begin at the upper right, circle counterclockwise around the broad rounded left body, and return into the right shoulder. Lift once. Descend the tall right spine and turn through its lower foot.

\subsection*{Writing — notice and trace}
Finger-trace the rounded body, lift, then trace the spine. Air-trace the same two runs.

\subsection*{Writing — copy with the model}
Copy visible \textbf{\gu{વ}} once. Check body, shoulder, spine; do not add a third run.

\subsection*{Writing — recall after hiding}
Hide \textbf{\gu{વ}}. Write \emph{va} once, uncover the model, and make at most one repair.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where is the lift? (\textbf{Between the rounded body and right spine.})

Sources: \href{https://www.t30apps.com/gujarati-alphabet-writing/}{Gujarati Alphabet Writing Practice} and the \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0A80.pdf}{Unicode Gujarati chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ya]{\gu{ય} — upper turn, lower body, separate spine, ya}

\label{lesson:GU-W02-ya}



\begin{quote}
Write \textbf{\gu{વ}} once from memory. Name its two runs, then move on.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — meet the shape}
Keep \textbf{\gu{ય}} visible. It is \textbf{ya}. Begin at the upper left, circle through the rounded upper turn, and sweep around the broad lower body into the long right shoulder. Lift once; descend the tall right spine and turn through its lower foot.

\subsection*{Writing — notice and trace}
Trace the body once with a finger, lift, then trace the spine. Repeat once in the air.

\subsection*{Writing — copy with the model}
Copy visible \textbf{\gu{ય}} once. Check upper turn, lower body, shoulder, spine.

\subsection*{Writing — recall after hiding}
Hide the model. Write \emph{ya} once, compare with \textbf{\gu{ય}}, and make one repair at most.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which part is separate? (\textbf{The tall right spine.})

Sources: \href{https://www.t30apps.com/gujarati-alphabet-writing/}{Gujarati Alphabet Writing Practice} and the \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0A80.pdf}{Unicode Gujarati chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bha]{\gu{ભ} — broad loop, inner turn, separate spine, bha}

\label{lesson:GU-W02-bha}



\begin{quote}
Write \textbf{\gu{ય}} once from memory. Check only its separate right spine.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — meet the shape}
Keep \textbf{\gu{ભ}} visible. It is \textbf{bha}, one consonant sound with the inherent \emph{a}. Begin at the lower left, circle clockwise around the broad loop, wind through the compact inner turn, and exit across the long right shoulder. Lift once; descend the tall right spine and turn through its lower foot.

\subsection*{Writing — notice and trace}
Finger-trace the loop-and-shoulder run once, lift, then trace the spine. Air-trace once.

\subsection*{Writing — copy with the model}
Copy visible \textbf{\gu{ભ}} once. Check broad loop, compact inner turn, shoulder, spine.

\subsection*{Writing — recall after hiding}
Hide \textbf{\gu{ભ}}. Write \emph{bha} once, uncover it, and repair one landmark if needed.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say the sound slowly. (\textbf{bha.}) How many pen-down runs? (\textbf{Two.})

Sources: \href{https://www.t30apps.com/gujarati-alphabet-writing/}{Gujarati Alphabet Writing Practice} and the \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0A80.pdf}{Unicode Gujarati chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dha]{\gu{ધ} — high entry, broad lower body, separate spine, dha}

\label{lesson:GU-W02-dha}



\begin{quote}
Write \textbf{\gu{ભ}} once. Point to its compact inner turn, then stop reviewing.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — meet the shape}
Keep \textbf{\gu{ધ}} visible. It is \textbf{dha}. Begin at the high left entry, descend through the upper turn and narrow middle, then sweep around the broad lower body into the right shoulder. Lift once; descend the tall right spine and turn through its foot.

\subsection*{Writing — notice and trace}
Finger-trace those two runs once. Air-trace them once, keeping the lift in place.

\subsection*{Writing — copy with the model}
Copy visible \textbf{\gu{ધ}} once. Check high entry, narrow middle, broad lower body, spine.

\subsection*{Writing — recall after hiding}
Hide the model. Write \emph{dha} once, uncover \textbf{\gu{ધ}}, and make one repair at most.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What narrows between the upper and lower bodies? (\textbf{The middle turn.})

Sources: \href{https://www.t30apps.com/gujarati-alphabet-writing/}{Gujarati Alphabet Writing Practice} and the \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0A80.pdf}{Unicode Gujarati chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[-ṛ]{\gu{ૃ} — a small below-consonant sign, -ṛ}

\label{lesson:GU-W02-vocalic-r}



\begin{quote}
Point to \textbf{\gu{ભ}}, then \textbf{\gu{ધ}}. Say \emph{bha}, then \emph{dha}. Do not copy either.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — meet the shape}
Keep \textbf{\gu{ૃ}} visible. This is not a free-standing letter. It is a small vowel sign placed \textbf{below a consonant}, mainly in Sanskrit loans, and it gives vocalic \emph{ṛ}. Keep \textbf{\gu{ભૃ}} visible: the new information is only the small sign below \textbf{\gu{ભ}}.

\subsection*{Writing — notice and trace}
Finger-trace the visible \textbf{\gu{ૃ}} once. No stroke-order claim is being added here; copy the printed model's small below-consonant shape.

\subsection*{Writing — copy with the model}
Keep \textbf{\gu{ભ}} visible. Copy only \textbf{\gu{ૃ}} beneath it once, making \textbf{\gu{ભૃ}}. Point to the base, then the sign, and say \emph{bhṛ}.

\subsection*{Writing — recall after hiding}
Hide only the sign while \textbf{\gu{ભ}} remains visible. Add it once, then compare with \textbf{\gu{ભૃ}}.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is \textbf{\gu{ૃ}} independent? (\textbf{No; it attaches below a consonant.}) Where will it appear next? (\textbf{Only in the old root bhṛ.})

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0A80.pdf}{Unicode Gujarati chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\gu{આભાર}]{\gu{આભાર} (ābhār) — \textquotedblleft{}thank you,\textquotedblright{} an obligation gladly owed}

\label{lesson:GU-C01-aabhaar}



\begin{quote}
Gujarati's everyday \textquotedblleft{}thank you\textquotedblright{} — and it comes from the idea of being \emph{indebted}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\gu{આ}} (the independent long \emph{ā}, for a word-initial vowel) + \textbf{\gu{ભા}} (\emph{bhā}) + \textbf{\gu{ર}} (\emph{r}) $\to$ \textbf{\gu{આભાર}} (\emph{ābhār}). Note again: no top line.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\gu{આભાર}} (\emph{ābhār}, \textquotedblleft{}thanks, gratitude\textquotedblright{}) is from Sanskrit \textbf{\gu{આભાર}} (\emph{ābhāra}, \textquotedblleft{}a burden, an obligation\textquotedblright{}), from \textbf{\gu{આ}-} (\emph{ā-}, \textquotedblleft{}toward\textquotedblright{}) + the root \textbf{\gu{ભૃ}} (\emph{bhṛ}, \textquotedblleft{}to bear, carry\textquotedblright{}). To thank someone is to acknowledge you now \emph{bear an obligation} to them — the same idea as English \textbf{oblige} (Latin \emph{ob-} + \emph{ligāre} \textquotedblleft{}to bind\textquotedblright{}) and Portuguese \emph{obrigado}. That root \emph{bhṛ} is Proto-Indo-European \textbf{*b\textsuperscript{h}er-}, the ancestor of English \textbf{bear} (to carry) and Latin \emph{ferre}. (The more Sanskritic \textbf{\gu{ધન્યવાદ}} \emph{dhanyavād} is also used, but \emph{ābhār} is the warm, everyday Gujarati word.)
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ābhār\textquotedblright{}
  \item what it literally acknowledges (an obligation \textquotedblleft{}borne\textquotedblright{})
  \item the English cousin of its root \emph{bhṛ} (\textbf{bear}, \textquotedblleft{}to carry\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Script retrieval}
Hide the earlier models. Write \textbf{\gu{ર}} once, then write the unattached practice model \textbf{\gu{ૃ}} once. Compare, repair only one mark if needed, and stop.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{ābhār} literally mean, and what English word shares its root? (\textquotedblleft{}An obligation borne\textquotedblright{}; \textbf{bear} — from PIE \emph{*b\textsuperscript{h}er-}, \textquotedblleft{}to carry.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\gu{આવજો}]{\gu{આવજો} (āvjo) — \textquotedblleft{}goodbye\textquotedblright{} (come again)}

\label{lesson:GU-C01-aavjo}



\begin{quote}
The everyday Gujarati goodbye — and, like the goodbyes across all of India, it is really an invitation to return.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\gu{આ}} (independent \emph{ā}) + \textbf{\gu{વ}} (\emph{va}) + \textbf{\gu{જો}} (\emph{jo}) $\to$ \textbf{\gu{આવજો}} (\emph{āvjo}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\gu{આવજો}} (\emph{āvjo}) is the polite imperative of \emph{āvvũ}, \textquotedblleft{}to come\textquotedblright{} — literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{{[}please{]} come {[}again{]}}.\textquotedblright{} A Gujarati never signs off by saying \textquotedblleft{}I'm leaving\textquotedblright{}; the parting word is \emph{come}. It is the same \textquotedblleft{}promise of return\textquotedblright{} that runs through the whole subcontinent — Tamil \emph{pōy varugiṟēṉ} (\textquotedblleft{}I'll go and come back\textquotedblright{}), Bengali \emph{āshi} (\textquotedblleft{}I'll come\textquotedblright{}), Hindi \emph{phir milenge} (\textquotedblleft{}we'll meet again\textquotedblright{}) — here made into a single warm word built on the verb \emph{to come}. (To one person, familiarly: \textbf{\gu{આવજે}} \emph{āvje}.)
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}āvjo\textquotedblright{}
  \item what it literally means (\textquotedblleft{}{[}please{]} come {[}again{]}\textquotedblright{})
  \item the verb it's built on (\emph{āvvũ}, \textquotedblleft{}to come\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Script retrieval}
Without looking back, write \textbf{\gu{દ}}, then \textbf{\gu{ય}}, one time each. Compare them with the earlier models. Repair one shape if needed; do not start a row.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the Gujarati goodbye literally say, and what verb is it from? (\textquotedblleft{}Come {[}again{]}\textquotedblright{}; \emph{āvvũ}, \textquotedblleft{}to come\textquotedblright{} — never \textquotedblleft{}I'm leaving.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\gu{હા} / \gu{ના}]{\gu{હા} / \gu{ના} (hā / nā) — \textquotedblleft{}yes\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GU-C01-haa-naa}



\begin{quote}
Two tiny words no conversation survives without — and one is a cousin of English.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\gu{હા}} (\emph{hā}) = \textbf{\gu{હ}} (\emph{ha}) + the long-\emph{ā} sign. \textbf{\gu{ના}} (\emph{nā}) = \textbf{\gu{ન}} (\emph{na}) + the long-\emph{ā} sign.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\gu{હા}} (\emph{hā}, \textquotedblleft{}yes\textquotedblright{}) and \textbf{\gu{ના}} (\emph{nā}, \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{}). The \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{} rides the ancient negative \textbf{na-} — the very same Proto-Indo-European \textbf{*ne} behind English \textbf{no}, \textbf{not}, \textbf{none}, Latin \emph{nōn}, Hindi \emph{nahīṁ}, and Bengali \emph{nā}. Of all the words in this book, this \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{} reaches furthest unchanged: one syllable spoken, in some form, from Iceland to Gujarat for five thousand years.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hā\textquotedblright{} (yes) and \textquotedblleft{}nā\textquotedblright{} (no)
  \item the shared ancestor of \emph{nā} and English \emph{no} (PIE \emph{*ne})
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Script retrieval}
Hide the earlier models. Write \textbf{\gu{ભ}}, then \textbf{\gu{વ}}, one time each. Compare the two shapes and repair only the one that needs it.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What ancient root links Gujarati \emph{nā} to English \emph{no}? (Proto-Indo- European \emph{*ne}, \textquotedblleft{}not.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hā]{\gu{હા} — one supported copy}

\label{lesson:GU-W01-haa-guided-copy}



\begin{quote}
Point to the consonant \textbf{\gu{હ}}, then the attached vowel sign \textbf{\gu{ા}}. Say the whole known word: \textbf{\gu{હા}}, \emph{hā}, \textquotedblleft{}yes.\textquotedblright{} Keep the model visible.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Writing — guided copy}
Copy \textbf{\gu{હા}} once. You may look back after each piece: first \textbf{\gu{હ}}, then \textbf{\gu{ા}}. Touch both pieces in your copy and read \emph{hā}.

\subsection*{Script retrieval — one older consonant}
Now hide the earlier model for \textbf{\gu{ધ}} and write it once. Compare and make at most one repair.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Compare only the two pieces and their order. Repair one piece if needed, then stop. The model stays visible today.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hā]{\gu{હા} — look, hide, write, compare}

\label{lesson:GU-W01-haa-delayed-copy}



\begin{quote}
Look at \textbf{\gu{હા}} for five seconds. Point first to \textbf{\gu{હ}}, then to \textbf{\gu{ા}}. Do not copy it yet.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Writing — delayed copy}
1. cover \textbf{\gu{હા}} 2. wait five seconds 3. write it once from memory 4. uncover the model and compare the two pieces

If one piece differs, circle it and repair only that place. Repair is part of the exercise, not a failure.

\subsection*{Script retrieval — one older vowel sign}
Hide the earlier model for \textbf{\gu{ૃ}}. Write the small below-consonant sign once, compare it, and stop after one repair.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Read your repaired word as \emph{hā}. Stop after one memory attempt.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hā]{One heard answer — write what you know}

\label{lesson:GU-W01-haa-dictation}



\begin{quote}
Cover the answer lower on this page. You will hear one familiar answer. No new Gujarati is hiding in this lesson.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Writing — short dictation}
{[}YOU HEAR: \emph{hā} — \textquotedblleft{}yes\textquotedblright{}{]}

Write the Gujarati word from sound alone. Now uncover and compare: \textbf{\gu{હા}}. Check \textbf{\gu{હ}} first and attached \textbf{\gu{ા}} second. Repair one place if needed.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Writing from sound completes this tiny runway. It is not a mock assessment; later lessons must grow from one known word to forms, messages, and timed tasks.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\gu{સારું}]{\gu{સારું} (sārũ) — \textquotedblleft{}good,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}okay\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GU-C01-saarun}



\begin{quote}
The all-purpose \textquotedblleft{}good / fine / okay / alright\textquotedblright{} — and your first taste of Gujarati's three genders.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\gu{સા}} (\emph{sā}) + \textbf{\gu{રું}} (\emph{rũ}, with the nasal \emph{anusvāra} on the \emph{u}) $\to$ \textbf{\gu{સારું}} (\emph{sārũ}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\gu{સારું}} (\emph{sārũ}, \textquotedblleft{}good, fine, okay\textquotedblright{}) is from Sanskrit \textbf{\gu{સાર}} (\emph{sāra}, \textquotedblleft{}essence, substance, the best part\textquotedblright{}) — the same \emph{sāra} behind Bengali's \emph{sāramilla} (\textquotedblleft{}no matter\textquotedblright{}). As \textquotedblleft{}okay/agreed\textquotedblright{} it oils every Gujarati conversation, the way English uses \textquotedblleft{}alright.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: three genders, on the adjective}]
Look at that ending \textbf{-\gu{ું}} (\emph{-ũ}). Gujarati, like Marathi, keeps \textbf{three} genders from Sanskrit — masculine, feminine, \textbf{and neuter} — where Hindi and Punjabi kept only two. An adjective agrees with its noun in all three:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\gu{સારો}} (\emph{sāro}) — masculine
  \item \textbf{\gu{સારી}} (\emph{sārī}) — feminine
  \item \textbf{\gu{સારું}} (\emph{sārũ}) — \textbf{neuter}
\end{itemize}

Standing alone as \textquotedblleft{}okay,\textquotedblright{} it takes the neuter \emph{sārũ}. You will meet this three-way agreement on every adjective and possessive.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}sārũ\textquotedblright{} — good / okay
  \item the three genders — \emph{sāro} (m.) / \emph{sārī} (f.) / \emph{sārũ} (n.)
  \item the Sanskrit root (\emph{sāra}, \textquotedblleft{}essence\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{sārũ} mean, and what does its \emph{-ũ} ending tell you? (\textquotedblleft{}Good / okay\textquotedblright{}; it is the \textbf{neuter} — Gujarati keeps three genders.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Chapter 2 — Courtesy and responses}

\label{lesson:GU-C01-practice}



\begin{quote}
No new words. The five greetings, mixed and recombined.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{How to answer — rapid recall}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item hello / goodbye — \emph{namaste}
  \item thank you — \emph{ābhār}
  \item yes and no — \emph{hā} / \emph{nā}
  \item good / okay — \emph{sārũ}
  \item the \textquotedblleft{}come again\textquotedblright{} goodbye — \emph{āvjo}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Script — the script and the language}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the one visible thing that sets Gujarati apart from Devanagari (no top line)
  \item how many genders Gujarati keeps (three — \emph{sāro/sārī/sārũ})
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing — three gentle retrievals}
Cover every written answer. Hear \emph{hā}, \textquotedblleft{}yes,\textquotedblright{} once in your mind and write it from memory. Then uncover \textbf{\gu{હા}} and check the two pieces: \textbf{\gu{હ}}, then attached \textbf{\gu{ા}}. One repair is allowed.

\textbf{Four consonants.}

Hide the models. Write \textbf{\gu{ર} \gu{દ} \gu{વ} \gu{ય}}, once each and in that order. Uncover the models and compare one shape at a time. Make no more than one repair per shape.

\textbf{Two consonants and one sign.}

Keep the models hidden. Write \textbf{\gu{ભ}}, then \textbf{\gu{ધ}}. Finally write \textbf{\gu{ભ}} again and attach \textbf{\gu{ૃ}} below it to make \textbf{\gu{ભૃ}}. Compare, repair, and stop.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built — roots you now carry}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{namaste} = \emph{namas} \textquotedblleft{}a bow\textquotedblright{} + \emph{te} \textquotedblleft{}to you\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{ābhār} $\leftarrow$ \emph{ā} + \emph{bhṛ} \textquotedblleft{}to bear\textquotedblright{} $\to$ an obligation borne (cousin of English \emph{bear})
  \item \emph{nā} (\textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ PIE \emph{*ne} $\to$ English \emph{no/not/none}
  \item \emph{āvjo} (\textquotedblleft{}goodbye\textquotedblright{}) = \textquotedblleft{}come {[}again{]},\textquotedblright{} from \emph{āvvũ} \textquotedblleft{}to come\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Someone thanks you and turns to leave. Answer their thanks and send them off the Gujarati way. (\emph{Sārũ} — and \emph{āvjo}, \textquotedblleft{}come again.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
